summary:
We developed the Western US Harmonized Burning Activity Calendar, an end-to-end data harmonization pipeline and interactive web application built on NASA FIRMS satellite detections. Because aging MODIS sensors (1 km resolution, 2000–present) are retiring alongside newer VIIRS instruments (375 m resolution, 2012–present), raw multi-decade fire records exhibit an artificial jump after 2012.
To resolve this discrepancy, our pipeline filters low-confidence anomalies and persistent industrial heat sources, bins detections onto uniform Uber H3 hexagonal grids (~3.2 km), assigns exact state boundaries via polygon matching, and trains seasonal Ridge regression models on overlapping MODIS–VIIRS observations to align historical MODIS active fire cells and Fire Radiative Power (MW) to the VIIRS baseline.
Our interactive Streamlit dashboard lets fire managers, researchers, and the public explore 26+ years of continuous wildfire activity via a clickable calendar heatmap, a date-range H3 map, a calibration validation tab, and a ±7-day climatological median baseline. Filtered results render interactively on the map and export directly as CSV files. This sensor-agnostic tool supports wildfire contingency and prevention planning and scales seamlessly across the entire United States, globally, and with expanded analytical capabilities.
details:
The Western US Harmonized Burning Activity Calendar is an end-to-end geospatial data pipeline and interactive web application that unifies 26+ years of NASA FIRMS satellite wildfire detections (MODIS, 2000–present, and VIIRS, 2012–present) into a single, sensor-agnostic historical record.

  • Automated Data Acquisition (fetch_firms.py): Pulls historical Standard Processing (SP) and Near Real-Time (NRT) thermal anomaly records across MODIS, VIIRS Suomi-NPP, and VIIRS NOAA-20 archives using a resumable, year-cached API downloader.
  • Noise & Industrial Filtering (harmonize_firms.py): Removes low-confidence detections, volcanoes, offshore platforms, and persistent year-round industrial heat sources (such as gas flares, refineries, and power plants active >60 days/year in the same location).
  • Spatial Normalization & Exact State Tagging: Bins raw coordinates onto uniform Uber H3 Resolution 6 hexagons (~3.2 km edge length) to eliminate multi-pixel inflation across sensors, and matches every detection to exact state borders across the 11 Western US states using prepared Shapely polygons.
  • Cross-Sensor Calibration & Climatological Baselines: Trains seasonal Ridge regression models on overlapping MODIS–VIIRS observations (2012–present) to calibrate historical MODIS active fire cells and Fire Radiative Power (MW) to the higher-resolution VIIRS baseline. It then computes a smoothed ±7-day multi-year median and daily Anomaly Ratio for every calendar day.
  • Interactive Exploration (DisplayTool.py): Displays a clickable daily burning activity calendar, a date-range H3 hotspot map with state boundary highlights, a historical median comparison chart, a sensor calibration validation tab (R² and RMSE metrics), and one-click CSV exports of user-filtered fire data.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Eliminates Sensor Transition Bias: Without calibration, VIIRS's 375 m resolution detects significantly more small and cool fires than MODIS's 1 km resolution, creating an artificial jump in fire activity after 2012. Harmonization ensures multi-decade trend lines reflect real environmental change rather than hardware upgrades.
  • Actionable Contingency & Prevention Planning: By normalizing daily fire activity against a ±7-day seasonal median, fire managers and researchers can immediately spot out-of-season fires (e.g., early spring or late autumn wind-driven events) and quantify regional surges.
  • Scalable Architecture: Designed with modular hexagonal indexing and polygon-based regional tagging, the platform scales seamlessly from the Western US to the entire United States and global fire-prone regions, while supporting future integrations like weather overlays or official perimeter datasets.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Programming Language: Python 3.9+
  • Data Processing & Machine Learning: pandas, numpy, scikit-learn (Ridge regression & validation metrics), requests
  • Geospatial Engineering: h3 (Uber H3 hexagonal spatial indexing), shapely (prepared point-in-polygon state boundary matching)
  • Frontend & Visualization: streamlit (interactive dashboard & Streamlit Community Cloud deployment), plotly (clickable calendar tile grid, vector geo maps, and time-series visualizations)
  • Data Sources: NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System) MODIS and VIIRS archives; US States GeoJSON boundary polygons
  • Development Environment: Local workstation (Windows/PowerShell) and GitHub for version control and cloud deployment.

What Makes Our Project Creative

  • Hexagonal Resolution Equalization: Rather than comparing raw point counts—where one fire produces multiple 375 m VIIRS pixels versus a single 1 km MODIS pixel—mapping both sensors onto a shared H3 hexagonal grid creates an apples-to-apples spatial unit before statistical calibration even begins.
  • Linked Calendar-to-Map Exploration: Pairing a GitHub-style daily contribution heatmap with an interactive date-range H3 map turns 26 years of dense satellite tables into an intuitive visual timeline where users can click any anomalous day or drag a multi-week siege window to inspect exact fire locations and download filtered CSVs.
  • Built-In Scientific Transparency: Including a dedicated Sensor Calibration Validation tab with live R², RMSE, and 1:1 parity plots lets users verify the calibration accuracy firsthand.

Key Factors Our Team Considered

  • Sensor Continuity & Satellite Retirement: Accounted for aging MODIS instruments approaching retirement as well as the November 2026 transition from VIIRS Suomi-NPP (VIIRS_SNPP_SP) to VIIRS NOAA-20 (VIIRS_NOAA20_SP/NRT). Solved the problem of differing sensor sensitivities by computed a best-fit scaling factor to perform conversions between MODIS and VIIRS values of fire radiant power.
  • False Positives from Industrial Activity: Separated true vegetation wildfires from static industrial heat sources by combining NASA's type == 0 classification with a 60-day annual persistence filter so NRT data remains clean.
  • Cloud & Smoke Obscuration: Tracked both clear-sky detection days and total elapsed episode spans (start_date to end_date) so multi-day wildfires obscured by heavy smoke are accurately represented.
  • API Rate Limits & Offline Reproducibility: Engineered resumable year-by-year caching in fetch_firms.py to stay safely within NASA FIRMS transaction limits and decouple heavy offline processing from lightweight cloud deployment.
